items.followUp: Define equilibrium and explain its second condition, giving one example.

rubric.why: Checks the definition’s force-balance requirement.
rubric.description: Defines equilibrium in terms of zero resultant force.
rubric.how: State that the net or resultant force on a body is zero.

rubric.why: Checks the rotational-balance requirement in the definition of equilibrium.
rubric.description: Includes the condition for rotational equilibrium.
rubric.how: State that the net torque (moment) is zero.

rubric.why: Checks an appropriate description of a body in equilibrium.
rubric.description: States that the body remains at rest or moves with uniform velocity.
rubric.how: Give either state of motion consistent with equilibrium.

rubric.why: Checks the first condition and its mathematical expression.
rubric.description: Explains the first condition of equilibrium and gives an example.
rubric.how: State that the vector sum of all forces is zero; illustrate with balanced forces, such as a book resting on a table.

modelAnswer: A body is in equilibrium when the resultant force and resultant torque acting on it are both zero.
For example, a book resting on a table is in equilibrium: its weight downward is balanced by the table’s upward force.
The first condition of equilibrium is that the vector sum of all forces acting on a body is zero: ΣF = 0.
For example, when equal forces act in opposite directions on a stationary object, they balance and the object has no acceleration.

items.followUp: An object weighs 24 N in air and 15 N when fully immersed in water. Calculate its density. Take the density of water as 1000 kg/m³.

rubric.why: Checks the weight in air is correctly identified from the question.
rubric.description: Identifies the weight in air as 18 N.
rubric.how: Use the stated weight in air as the numerator in the density calculation.

rubric.why: Checks the loss of weight, which equals the upthrust, is correctly calculated.
rubric.description: Finds the loss of weight in water as 6.6 N.
rubric.how: Subtract the immersed weight from the weight in air.

accept: density=weight in air/(weight in air-weight in water)
rubric.why: Checks the correct relationship between the object’s density and water’s density is used.
rubric.description: Uses the density relation based on weight and loss of weight.
rubric.how: Write ρobject = [Wair/(Wair − Wwater)] ρwater.

rubric.why: Checks the numerical calculation and final density with a suitable unit.
rubric.description: Calculates and reports the object’s density.
rubric.how: Substitute the given values and give the result in kg/m³ (or an equivalent density unit).

modelAnswer: Given: Weight in air, Wₐ = 18 N; weight in water, Ww = 11.4 N; density of water, ρw = 1000 kg/m³.
Loss in weight = Wₐ − Ww = 18 N − 11.4 N = 6.6 N.
Formula: ρobject = [Wₐ / (Wₐ − Ww)] ρw.
Substitution: ρobject = (18 N / 6.6 N) × 1000 kg/m³.
Answer: ρobject ≈ 2.73 × 10³ kg/m³.

items.followUp: What does plasma physics study, and what does geophysics study?

rubric.why: Checks the defining subject matter of plasma physics.
rubric.description: Defines plasma physics as the study of plasma or ionized gases.
rubric.how: Mention plasma, an ionized gas, as the subject studied.

rubric.why: Checks the defining subject matter of geophysics.
rubric.description: Defines geophysics as the study of Earth’s physical properties or processes.
rubric.how: Mention Earth and its physical properties or processes.

modelAnswer: Plasma physics is the branch of physics that studies plasma, an ionized gas, and its properties and behaviour.
Geophysics is the branch of physics that studies the physical properties and processes of the Earth.

items.followUp: State the least count of a typical screw gauge and explain how it helps measure small thicknesses accurately.

rubric.why: Checks the key reason for the screw gauge’s greater accuracy.
rubric.description: States that a screw gauge has a smaller least count than vernier callipers.
rubric.how: Compare the instruments’ least counts and note the screw gauge’s smaller value.

rubric.why: Checks that the smaller least count enables finer measurement.
rubric.description: Explains that the screw gauge can resolve smaller differences in length or thickness.
rubric.how: Connect the smaller least count to more precise measurement.

modelAnswer: A screw gauge has a smaller least count than vernier callipers (typically about 0.01 mm).
It can therefore measure smaller changes in thickness and gives a more precise reading.

items.followUp: Define the coefficient of friction and write its mathematical expression using limiting friction and normal reaction.

rubric.why: Checks that the coefficient is defined as a ratio of the relevant forces.
rubric.description: Defines the coefficient of friction as the ratio of limiting friction to normal reaction.
rubric.how: Identify limiting friction as the numerator and normal reaction as the denominator.

rubric.why: Checks the mathematical form is given correctly.
rubric.description: Writes the formula for the coefficient of friction.
rubric.how: Write μ = F/R, where F is limiting friction and R is normal reaction.

modelAnswer: The coefficient of friction is the ratio of limiting friction to the normal reaction between two surfaces.
Mathematically, μ = F/R, where F is the limiting friction and R is the normal reaction.

items.followUp: What is nuclear energy, and name one process in which it is released.

rubric.why: Checks that the answer identifies nuclear energy as energy associated with the atomic nucleus or nuclear reactions.
rubric.description: Defines nuclear energy in terms of the nucleus or nuclear reactions.
rubric.how: State that it is energy released from or associated with changes in an atomic nucleus.

rubric.why: Checks a valid description of how nuclear energy is released.
rubric.description: Mentions mass–energy conversion or a nuclear process such as fission or fusion.
rubric.how: Name fission or fusion, or state that some mass is converted into energy.

modelAnswer: Nuclear energy is the energy released in a nuclear reaction when the nucleus of an atom changes.
It is released in processes such as nuclear fission or fusion, in which some mass is converted into energy.

items.followUp: Use Newton’s law of gravitation to explain why the gravitational pull between two small objects is difficult to notice.

rubric.why: Checks the reason everyday objects exert only a weak gravitational attraction.
rubric.description: States that the masses of ordinary objects are small.
rubric.how: Explain that the masses involved in everyday situations are small.

rubric.why: Checks that the resulting force is too weak to be perceived.
rubric.description: Explains that the gravitational force is extremely small and cannot be felt.
rubric.how: Connect the small masses (and the very small gravitational constant) to an imperceptible force.

modelAnswer: The masses of objects around us are small, and the gravitational constant is very small.
Therefore, the gravitational force between everyday objects is extremely weak, so we do not feel it.
